paragraphs: It seems that people use two quite different standards when they publicly assess *a the actions of others. Sometimes they judge by the simple ideas of right and wrong found everywhere in the world; at other times they defer to a few very particular ideas that belong only to a certain age and country. These two standards often differ, and sometimes they conflict. Yet neither ever fully merges with the other or fully cancels it. At the height of its power, honor governs men’s will more than their belief. Even as they obey its commands without hesitation or complaint, they sense, by a faint but powerful instinct, a more general, more ancient and more sacred law, which they sometimes break but never stop acknowledging. Some actions have been considered virtuous and dishonorable at once; refusing to fight a duel is an example.

[Footnote a: The word “honor” does not always carry the same meaning, in French or in English. I. First, it means the dignity, glory or reverence a man receives from other people; in this sense a man is said to earn honor. 2. It also means the whole set of rules by which that dignity, glory or reverence is gained. So we say that a man has always strictly obeyed the laws of honor, or that a man has violated his honor. In this chapter the word is always used in the second sense.]

I think these peculiarities can be explained otherwise than by the mere whims of particular individuals and nations, which until now has been the usual way of reasoning on the subject. Humanity has general and lasting needs, and these have given rise to moral laws. Everywhere and always, people have attached blame and shame to neglecting those laws: breaking them was “to do ill,” and “to do well” was to follow them. Within this vast association of the human race, smaller associations have formed, which are called nations; and within those nations, further divisions have taken the names of classes or castes. Each of these associations is, so to speak, a separate kind of human being. It differs in no essential way from the mass of humanity, yet to some extent it stands apart and has needs of its own. These special needs account for the changes, varying in degree from country to country, in how human actions are viewed and in the judgment that ought to be passed on them. It is the general and permanent interest of mankind that people should not kill one another; but it may happen to be the particular and temporary interest of a people or a class to justify homicide, or even to honor it.

Honor is simply the particular rule, grounded in a particular state of society, by which a people or a class hands out praise or blame. Nothing is less fruitful to the mind than an abstract idea, so I hurry to bring in facts and examples to show what I mean.

For my illustration I choose the most extraordinary kind of honor the world has ever known, and the one we know best: aristocratic honor, which grew out of feudal society. I shall explain it through the principle I have laid down, and I shall explain the principle through this illustration. I will not ask here when and how the aristocracy of the Middle Ages arose, why it was so sharply cut off from the rest of the nation, or what founded and strengthened its power. I take its existence as established, and I am trying to account for the peculiar view it took of most human actions. What strikes me first is that in the feudal world actions were not always praised or blamed according to their intrinsic worth. Sometimes they were valued solely by reference to the person who did them or to whom they were done, which offends the general conscience of mankind. Thus certain actions that meant nothing coming from a man of humble station dishonored a noble, and others changed their whole character depending on whether the person wronged belonged to the aristocracy. When these distinctions first arose, the nobility was a separate body among the people, ruling them from the unreachable heights where it had entrenched itself. To keep this distinct position, which was the source of its strength, it needed not only political privileges but also a standard of right and wrong made for its own use. That a particular virtue or vice should belong to the nobility rather than to the humble classes, and that certain actions should be harmless when they touched a villein but criminal when they touched a noble, were often arbitrary matters. But that honor or shame should attach to a man’s actions according to his condition was a result of the inner structure of an aristocratic community. This has indeed been the case in every country that has had an aristocracy; as long as any trace of the principle survives, these peculiarities will persist. To debauch a woman of color hardly harms an American’s reputation; to marry her dishonors him.

In some cases feudal honor demanded revenge and branded forgiveness of insults as shameful; in others it sternly ordered men to master their own passions and to forget themselves. It did not make humanity or kindness its law, but it praised generosity; it valued open-handedness above benevolence; it allowed men to get rich by gambling or war, but not by work; it preferred great crimes to small earnings; it was less repelled by covetousness than by miserliness; it often sanctioned violence, but always condemned cunning and treachery as contemptible. These fantastic ideas did not come solely from the whims of those who held them. A class that has placed itself at the head of all others and above them, and that constantly strains to keep that high position, must honor above all the virtues that stand out for dignity and splendor and that combine easily with pride and love of power. Such men would not hesitate to turn the natural order of conscience upside down in order to put those virtues ahead of all others. One can even imagine that some of the bolder and more brilliant vices would readily be ranked above the quiet, unassuming virtues. The mere existence of such a class in society makes these things unavoidable.

The nobles of the Middle Ages ranked military courage first among the virtues, and made it stand in place of many of them. This too was a peculiar opinion, and it arose necessarily from the peculiar state of society. Feudal aristocracy lived by war and for war. Arms had founded its power, and arms maintained it. It therefore needed nothing beyond military courage, and that quality was naturally raised above all others. Whatever showed it, even at the expense of reason and humanity, was approved and often required by the customs of the time. That was the main principle; human whim can be traced only in the smaller details. That a man should take a tap on the cheek as an unbearable insult, and be obliged to kill in single combat the person who struck him so lightly, is an arbitrary rule. But that a noble could not calmly accept an insult, and was dishonored if he took a blow without fighting, were direct consequences of the basic principles and needs of a military aristocracy.

So it was true, to a certain extent, to say that the laws of honor were capricious; but those caprices always stayed within certain necessary limits. What our forefathers called honor is so far from being an arbitrary law in my eyes that I would readily undertake to trace its most incoherent and fantastic demands to a small number of fixed, unchanging needs inherent in feudal society.

If I followed the idea of feudal honor into politics, I should find its dictates no harder to explain. The social state and political institutions of the Middle Ages were such that the nation’s supreme power never governed the community directly. In the people’s eyes that power did not exist. Each man looked up to a particular individual whom he was bound to obey, and through that intermediary he was connected to everyone else. So in feudal society the whole system of the commonwealth rested on the feeling of fidelity to the person of the lord, and to destroy that feeling was to open the floodgates of anarchy. Moreover, all members of the aristocracy had constant occasion to appreciate how important fidelity to a political superior was, since each of them was a vassal as well as a lord and had to command as well as obey. To stay faithful to the lord, to sacrifice oneself for him if called upon, to share his good or bad fortune, to stand by him in his undertakings whatever they were: these were the first demands of feudal honor in relation to the political institutions of those times. Public opinion branded a vassal’s treachery with extraordinary severity, and a name of particular infamy, “felony,” was coined for the offense.

By contrast, one finds few traces in the Middle Ages of the passion that gave life to the nations of antiquity, I mean patriotism; the word itself is not very old in the language. *b Feudal institutions hid the country as a whole from men’s sight and made love of it less necessary. The nation was forgotten in the passions that bound men to persons. So remaining faithful to one’s country was no part of the strict law of feudal honor. This is not to say that love of country did not exist in our forefathers’ hearts; but it was a dim, feeble instinct, which has grown clearer and stronger as aristocratic classes have been abolished and the nation’s supreme power centralized. One can see this plainly in the opposite judgments that European nations have passed on events in their histories, depending on the generation making them. What most dishonored the Constable de Bourbon in his contemporaries’ eyes was that he took up arms against his king; what most dishonors him in ours is that he made war on his country. We condemn him as harshly as our forefathers did, but for different reasons.
[Footnote b: French writers did not use even the word “patrie” until the sixteenth century.]

I have taken the honor of feudal times to illustrate my point because its features are more sharply marked, and more familiar to us, than those of any other period. But I could have chosen an example elsewhere and reached the same conclusion by another road. We know the Romans less well than our own ancestors, yet we know that they had certain peculiar ideas of glory and disgrace, which did not derive solely from the general principles of right and wrong. Many human actions were judged differently depending on whether they affected a Roman citizen or a stranger, a freeman or a slave; certain vices were publicly proclaimed, and certain virtues were praised above all others. “In that age,” says Plutarch in the life of Coriolanus, “martial prowess was more honored and prized in Rome than all the other virtues, insomuch that it was called virtus, the name of virtue itself, by applying the name of the kind to this particular species; so that virtue in Latin was as much as to say valor.” Can anyone fail to recognize the particular need of that singular community, which was formed to conquer the world?

Any nation would give us similar grounds for observation. As I have already remarked, whenever men gather as a distinct community, the notion of honor immediately grows up among them, that is, a system of opinions of their own about what deserves blame or praise; and these special rules always originate in the community’s special habits and interests. To a certain extent this applies to democratic communities as well as to others, as we shall now prove by the example of the Americans. *c Some vague ideas of the old aristocratic honor of Europe can still be found scattered among Americans’ opinions. But these inherited opinions are few, they have little root in the country, and little power. They are like a religion that still has some temples standing, though men have stopped believing in it. Yet amid these half-erased notions of foreign honor, some new opinions have sprung up, which make up what may be called, in our day, American honor. I have shown how the Americans are constantly driven into commerce and industry. Their origin, their social condition, their political institutions, and even the place they live all push them irresistibly in this direction. Their present condition, then, is that of an almost exclusively manufacturing and commercial association, set in the midst of a new and boundless country, which their chief aim is to explore for profit. This is the trait that most distinguishes the American people from all others at present. All the quiet virtues that give the community a regular movement and encourage business will therefore be held in particular honor by that people, and neglecting them will bring public contempt. All the more turbulent virtues, which often dazzle but more often disturb society, will on the contrary rank lower in this same people’s estimation. They may be neglected without losing the community’s esteem; acquiring them would perhaps risk losing it.
[Footnote c: By “the Americans” I mean here those who live in the States without slavery; they alone can be said to offer a complete picture of democratic society.]

The Americans classify men’s vices in a way that is just as arbitrary. There are certain propensities that seem blameworthy to universal reason and to the conscience of all mankind, but that happen to suit the particular and temporary needs of the American community. These are only lightly reproved, and sometimes even encouraged. The love of wealth and the lesser propensities connected with it are the clearest example. To clear, to farm and to transform the vast uninhabited continent that is his domain, the American needs the daily support of an energetic passion, and that passion can only be the love of wealth. So the passion for wealth is not condemned in America, and as long as it does not go beyond the limits set for public safety, it is held in honor. The American praises as a noble and praiseworthy ambition what our own forefathers in the Middle Ages branded as servile greed, just as he treats the ardor for conquest and the martial temper that drove them to battle as a blind and barbarous frenzy. In the United States fortunes are lost and regained without difficulty; the country is boundless and its resources inexhaustible. The people have all the needs and cravings of a growing creature, and whatever their efforts, they are always surrounded by more than they can take. What would be fatal to such a people is not the ruin of a few individuals, which can soon be repaired, but the inactivity and sloth of the community at large. Boldness in enterprise is the chief cause of its rapid progress, its strength and its greatness. Commercial business there is like a vast lottery, in which a small number of men constantly lose, but the state always gains; such a people ought therefore to encourage and honor boldness in commercial speculation. But any bold speculation risks the fortune of the speculator and of all who trust him. The Americans, who make a virtue of commercial recklessness, have no right in any case to brand with disgrace those who practice it. Hence the strange indulgence shown to bankrupts in the United States; their honor does not suffer from such a misfortune. In this respect the Americans differ not only from the nations of Europe but from all the commercial nations of our time, and accordingly they resemble none of them in their position or their needs.

In America, all the vices that tend to impair purity of morals and destroy the marriage bond are treated with a severity unknown in the rest of the world. At first sight this seems strangely at odds with the tolerance shown there on other subjects, and one is surprised to find such relaxed and such strict morality in the same people. But these things are less incoherent than they seem. Public opinion in the United States represses very gently the love of wealth that promotes the nation’s commercial greatness and prosperity, and it especially condemns the looseness of morals that turns the human mind from the pursuit of well-being and disrupts the internal order of home life, which is so necessary to business success. To win the esteem of their fellow citizens, Americans are therefore forced to adopt orderly habits, and in this sense it may be said that they make it a point of honor to live chastely.

On one point American honor agrees with the ideas of honor recognized in Europe: it ranks courage as the highest virtue and treats it as the greatest of man’s moral necessities. But the idea of courage itself takes on a different look. In the United States military valor is little prized. The courage best known and most esteemed is the kind that makes men brave the dangers of the ocean to reach port sooner, endure the hardships of the wilderness without complaint, and bear a solitude more cruel than hardship. It is the courage that leaves them almost unmoved by the loss of a fortune laboriously acquired, and instantly drives them to fresh efforts to make another. This kind of courage is particularly necessary to the maintenance and prosperity of the American communities, and they hold it in particular honor and esteem; to show a lack of it is to incur certain disgrace.

I have one more characteristic point that may bring out the idea of this chapter more strongly. In a democratic society like that of the United States, where fortunes are small and insecure, everybody works, and work opens the way to everything. This has turned the point of honor completely around and set it against idleness. In America I have sometimes met wealthy young men who personally disliked any laborious effort but had been forced to take up a profession. Their disposition and their fortune would have allowed them to stay without employment, but public opinion forbade it, too imperiously to be disobeyed. In the European countries, by contrast, where aristocracy is still struggling against the flood that is overwhelming it, I have often seen men, constantly spurred by their needs and desires, remain idle so as not to lose the esteem of their equals; and I have known them to put up with boredom and hardship rather than work. No one can fail to see that these opposite obligations are two different rules of conduct, both nevertheless originating in the notion of honor.

What our forefathers called honor without qualification was really only one of its forms; they gave a general name to what was only one kind. Honor is therefore found in democratic ages as well as aristocratic ones, but it will not be hard to show that it looks different in the former. Not only are its injunctions different; as we shall shortly see, they are fewer and less precise, and its dictates are obeyed less strictly. The position of a caste is always much more peculiar than that of a people. Nothing is so far from the ordinary world as a small community always made up of the same families (as the aristocracy of the Middle Ages was, for example), whose aim is to concentrate and keep education, wealth and power exclusively and hereditarily among its own members. But the further a community’s position departs from the ordinary, the more numerous its special needs are, and the more extensive its notions of honor corresponding to those needs. The rules of honor will therefore always be fewer among a people not divided into castes than among any other. If nations ever come into being in which it is even hard to find any distinct classes of society, the notion of honor will be limited to a small number of precepts, more and more in accord with the moral laws adopted by the mass of mankind. Thus the laws of honor will be less peculiar and less varied among a democratic people than in an aristocracy. They will also be more obscure, which follows necessarily from what precedes; for if the distinguishing marks of honor are fewer and less peculiar, they must often be hard to tell apart. Other reasons can be added. Among the aristocratic nations of the Middle Ages, generation followed generation in vain; each family was like a man who never dies and never moves, and opinions changed hardly more than conditions did. Everyone then had the same objects always before his eyes, viewed from the same point; his eyes gradually picked out the smallest details, and his discernment could not fail in the end to become clear and accurate. So the men of feudal times not only held very extraordinary opinions on matters of honor, but each of those opinions was present to their minds in a clear and precise form.

This can never happen in America, where all men are in constant motion, and where society, transformed daily by its own workings, changes its opinions along with its needs. In such a country people catch glimpses of the rules of honor, but they rarely have time to fix their attention on them.

But even if society stood still, it would still be hard to settle what the word “honor” ought to mean. In the Middle Ages each class had its own honor, so the same opinion was never held at the same time by a large number of men. This made it possible to give honor a fixed and exact form, all the more easily because everyone who held it, being in a perfectly identical and highly particular position, was naturally inclined to agree on the points of a law made for themselves alone. Thus the code of honor became a complete and detailed system in which everything was anticipated and provided for in advance, and a fixed and always visible standard was applied to human actions. Among a democratic nation like the Americans, where ranks are merged and the whole of society forms one single mass, made of elements that are all alike though not entirely identical, it is impossible ever to agree beforehand on what the laws of honor will or will not allow. Among that people, indeed, some national needs do exist that give rise to opinions on points of honor shared by the whole nation; but these opinions never occur at the same time, in the same way, or with the same intensity to the minds of the whole community. The law of honor exists, but it has no organs to proclaim it.

The confusion is greater still in a democratic country like France. There the different classes that made up the former fabric of society have been brought together but not yet blended, and day by day they bring into one another’s circles various and sometimes conflicting notions of honor. Every man, at his own will and pleasure, abandons one part of his forefathers’ creed and keeps another. Amid so many arbitrary choices no common rule can ever be established, and it is almost impossible to predict which actions will be held in honor and which will be thought disgraceful. Such times are wretched, but they do not last long.

Because honor among democratic nations is imperfectly defined, its influence is naturally weaker; it is hard to apply with certainty and firmness a law that is not distinctly known. Public opinion, the natural and supreme interpreter of the laws of honor, cannot clearly see which way blame or approval should lean, and so can only pass a hesitant judgment. Sometimes public opinion may contradict itself; more often it does not act and lets things pass.

The weakness of the sense of honor in democracies also arises from several other causes. In aristocratic countries the same notions of honor are always held by only a few people, always limited in number, and often set apart from their fellow citizens. In their minds honor is easily mingled and identified with everything that distinguishes their own position; it appears to them as the chief characteristic of their own rank. They apply its various rules with all the warmth of personal interest, and they feel (if I may use the expression) a passion for complying with its dictates. This truth is plain in the old black-letter lawbooks on “trial by battel.” The nobles in their disputes were bound to use the lance and sword, whereas the villeins used only sticks among themselves, “inasmuch as,” in the words of the old books, “villains have no honor.” This did not mean, as one might imagine today, that these people were contemptible, but simply that their actions were not to be judged by the same rules as the actions of the aristocracy.

At first sight it is surprising that when the sense of honor is at its strongest, its injunctions are usually at their strangest, so that the further honor is from common reason, the better it is obeyed. From this some have inferred that the laws of honor gained strength from their own extravagance. The two things do spring from the same source, but one is not derived from the other. Honor becomes fantastic in proportion to the peculiarity of the needs it expresses and the smallness of the number of men who feel them; and it is because it expresses needs of this kind that its influence is great. So the notion of honor is not stronger for being fantastic; it is fantastic and strong from one and the same cause.

Furthermore, among aristocratic nations each rank is different but all ranks are fixed. Every man occupies a place in his own sphere that he cannot leave, and he lives there among other men bound by the same ties. Among these nations no man can hope or fear to escape notice. No one is placed so low that he lacks a stage of his own, and no one can avoid blame or applause through obscurity. In democratic states, by contrast, where all members of the community are mixed together in the same crowd and in constant agitation, public opinion has no hold on men; they vanish at every moment and slip out of its power. Consequently the dictates of honor will be less imperious and less stringent there, for honor acts solely for the public eye, differing in this from mere virtue, which lives on itself, content with its own approval.

If the reader has clearly grasped all that precedes, he will understand that there is a close and necessary relation between inequality of social conditions and what has here been called honor, a relation that, if I am not mistaken, had not been clearly pointed out before. I shall therefore make one more attempt to illustrate it satisfactorily. Suppose a nation stands apart from the rest of mankind. Besides certain general needs inherent in the human race, it will have needs and interests peculiar to itself. At once certain opinions of blame or approval arise in the community that are its own, and that the members of the community call honor. Now suppose that in this same nation a caste arises that in its turn stands apart from all the other classes and acquires certain peculiar needs, which in turn give rise to special opinions. The honor of this caste, made up of a mixture of the nation’s peculiar notions and the caste’s still more peculiar ones, will be as far removed as can be imagined from the simple and general opinions of men.

Having reached this extreme point of the argument, I now turn back. When ranks are mingled and privileges abolished, the men who make up a nation become equal and alike once more. Their interests and needs become identical, and all the peculiar notions that each caste called honor gradually disappear. The notion of honor then comes from no source other than the needs peculiar to the nation at large, and it shows the world that nation’s individual character. Finally, if one may suppose that all the races of mankind were mingled, and that all the peoples of the earth came in the end to have the same interests and the same needs, with no characteristic peculiarities to tell them apart, then no conventional value at all would be attached to men’s actions. All would be viewed by all in the same light; the general necessities of mankind, revealed by conscience to every man, would become the common standard. Only the simple and general notions of right and wrong would then be recognized in the world, and by a natural and necessary tie the idea of blame or approval would be attached to them. Thus, to sum up my whole meaning in a single proposition: the dissimilarities and inequalities among men gave rise to the notion of honor; that notion weakens as those differences are wiped out, and with them it would disappear.
